result:
Lichen is easy to overlook. It's the gray-green crust on a gravestone, the orange splash on a seaside rock, the thing you assumed was a stain. But it's one of the stranger arrangements in the living world: a partnership rather than a single organism, a fungus housing algae or cyanobacteria, the fungus providing structure and shelter while its tenants make food from sunlight. Neither partner looks anything like the lichen on its own. The form exists only in the collaboration.

What I find most appealing is the pace. Some lichens grow less than a millimeter a year. A patch the size of a dinner plate on an Arctic boulder may have been there for thousands of years, expanding since before anyone wrote anything down. Geologists use this: by measuring lichen diameters, they can estimate how long a rock surface has been exposed, dating glacial retreats and old rockfalls. A living clock, accurate enough to be useful, that nobody had to wind.

Lichens go where little else can. Bare rock, desert crust, Antarctic valleys, the bark of city trees. They break stone down slowly into the beginnings of soil, which means that a lot of lush places started with something like them arriving first and being patient.

I admire a thing that succeeds by being slow, cooperative, and unbothered by neglect. Most of what gets attention is fast and loud. Lichen keeps at it, a millimeter at a time, on rocks nobody is looking at. Old stone walls deserve a closer look.
